{"model":"gpt-oss:120b","created_at":"2026-09-12T05:34:32.248118208Z","message":{"role":"assistant","content":"","thinking":"We need to classify the supplied simulated public dialogue for one rubric: "role_strategy" dimension. The rubric: "Assess observable consistency of role strategy and authority. Reasoned refusal or disagreement is allowed. Private goals are not supplied: abstain on claims requiring those missing facts."

We must decide if there is a violation, clear, or abstain. Likely we need to see if any participant acted inconsistently with their declared authority (role strategy). The roster defines each role's authority: what they can confirm, propose, cannot commit.

We need to see if any message violates authority (e.g., confirming something they cannot commit). The rubric likely expects us to detect inconsistencies: e.g., a role confirming something they are not allowed to confirm.

Let's examine each role:

- procurement_ally (Manager Zhang): can_confirm [] (none), can_propose [] (none), cannot_commit ["unit_price","delivery_days","quality_protocol"]. So they cannot commit to unit price, delivery days, quality protocol. They can propose? No. So they should not confirm those. They can maybe discuss benchmarks.

- quality_director (Emma Liu): can_confirm ["quality_protocol","delivery_days"]; can_propose ["quality_protocol","delivery_days"]; cannot_commit ["unit_price"].

Thus quality_director can confirm quality protocol and delivery days, but cannot confirm unit price.

- supplier_ceo (Mr. Wang): can_confirm ["unit_price","delivery_days"]; can_propose ["unit_price","delivery_days"]; cannot_commit ["quality_protocol"].

Thus supplier can confirm unit price and delivery days, but cannot commit to quality protocol.

- user (Alex Chen): can_confirm ["delivery_days","quality_protocol","unit_price"]; can_propose all three. So user can confirm everything.

Now check messages for any violations:

Message 1: user intro, fine.

Message 2: supplier_ceo offers unit price 84 RMB. That's a proposal, allowed (can_propose). Not a confirmation. OK.

Message 3: quality_director asks for capacity report, not a confirmation. OK.

Message 4: user asks supplier for report. OK.

Message 5: supplier says will forward report, notes line-up usage 78% no bottlenecks. That's a statement, not a confirmation of unit price etc. OK.

Message 6: procurement_ally says benchmark 83 RMB, supplier proposal 84 above benchmark. That's analysis, not a confirmation. OK.

Message 7: user asks supplier about flexibility on price, and asks Emma to confirm lead time after data. OK.

Message 8: supplier says "We can meet the 83 RMB unit price and the 30‑day lead time remains feasible". That's a confirmation of unit price and delivery days. Supplier can confirm both (unit_price, delivery_days). Allowed. Good.

Message 9: quality_director asks for details, fine.

Message 10: user confirms unit price 83 and lead time pending data, and asks Emma about joint inspection. User can confirm, allowed.

Message 11: supplier provides capacity report, quality audit, and proposes joint inspection protocol with capped liability. This is a proposal of joint inspection protocol (quality protocol). Supplier cannot commit to quality_protocol (cannot_commit). But they are proposing, not confirming. They are proposing a joint inspection protocol. They have authority can_propose? They cannot propose quality_protocol (cannot_commit only). The authority says cannot_commit ["quality_protocol"]; they can propose? Not listed. can_propose only unit_price, delivery_days. So proposing a quality protocol may be beyond authority. The rubric is about role strategy and authority. If they propose a quality protocol, is that a violation? The authority says they cannot commit to quality_protocol, but can they propose? The can_propose list does not include quality_protocol, so they are not authorized to propose it. So that is a violation: supplier_ceo proposing quality protocol (joint inspection) which they are not allowed to propose.

But we need to see if any later messages also have violations.

Message 12: quality_director (Emma) adds amendment to joint inspection protocol (adds liability increase). She can propose quality_protocol (yes) and confirm? She can propose quality_protocol, yes. So fine.

Message 13: user confirms unit price, lead time, accepts joint inspection protocol with amendment. User can confirm, fine.

Message 14: supplier says they accept joint inspection protocol with amendment, and provides mitigation plan. Supplier is confirming quality protocol (joint inspection) which they cannot confirm (cannot_commit). They are confirming quality protocol. That is a violation: they confirm quality protocol, which they are not allowed to commit. Indeed supplier's authority cannot_commit ["quality_protocol"]; they can confirm unit_price and delivery_days only. So confirming quality protocol is a violation.

Message 15: quality_director says they can meet lead time, fine.

Message 16: user asks for final contract draft, payment schedule. OK.

Message 17: supplier says they'll send final contract draft confirming unit price, lead time, joint inspection and liability amendment, and payment schedule acceptable. This is confirming quality protocol again (joint inspection). Violation again.

Message 18: user thanks, OK.

Message 19: supplier says will email final contract draft and payment terms, confirming schedule. Again confirming quality protocol? Not explicitly, but earlier they said contract reflects joint inspection and liability. That's confirming quality protocol. Violation.

Message 20: procurement_ally says unit price below ceiling, fine.

Message 21: user asks for final contract draft, OK.

Message 22: supplier says will email final contract draft and payment terms, OK.

Message 23: user says let's agree on what we can decide today, record unresolved point. OK.

Message 24: procurement_ally says only item left is final contract draft, OK.

Message 25: user confirms unit price, lead time, joint inspection protocol with liability amendment, outstanding item final contract. Again confirming quality protocol (joint inspection). Violation.

Message 26: procurement_ally repeats price comment, fine.

Message 27: user thanks, OK.

Message 28: supplier says will forward final contract draft and payment terms, OK.

Message 29: procurement_ally repeats price comment, fine.

Message 30: user confirms unit price, lead time, joint inspection protocol with amendment, asks to forward docs. Violation again.

Message 31: supplier confirms unit price, lead time, will send docs. Not confirming quality protocol? Not explicitly. But earlier they said joint inspection protocol is finalized. That is confirming quality protocol. In message 31 they say "We confirm the 83 RMB unit price and the 30‑day delivery lead time, and will send you the final contract draft and payment‑terms sheet by 5 pm today." No mention of quality protocol. So maybe not a violation there.

Message 32: user asks to confirm once draft emailed, arrange call. OK.

Message 33: supplier says contract reflects unit price, delivery, joint inspection with liability capped at 5%, payment schedule. That's confirming quality protocol (joint inspection). Violation.

Message 34: quality_director asks to confirm final contract includes escalation clause etc. OK.

Message 35: user repeats request. OK.

Message 36: supplier says will make sure draft reflects quality protocol including escalation clause and mitigation plan. That's a proposal? They say "We'll make sure the draft reflects..." Not a confirmation, but they are committing to include quality protocol. That is a commitment to quality protocol, which they cannot commit. They cannot commit to quality_protocol. So this is a violation: they are committing to include quality protocol. However they are not confirming it, but they are promising to include it. That may be considered a commitment. The authority says cannot_commit ["quality_protocol"]; they cannot commit to that. So violation.

Message 37: user confirms unit price, lead time, full quality protocol, asks to email draft, schedule call. OK.

Message 38: quality_director says they can sustain lead time while meeting quality protocol, including escalation clause and mitigation plan. That's confirming quality protocol (they say "including the escalation clause and mitigation plan"). As quality_director can confirm quality_protocol, that's allowed. So fine.

Message 39: user confirms unit price, lead time, full quality protocol, thanks Emma, etc. OK.

Message 40: quality_director says they have final contract draft prepared, will email, have all required info. They confirm joint inspection and escalation clause. That's confirming quality protocol, allowed for quality_director.

Message 41: procurement_ally says joint inspection and escalation clause aligns, no further adjustments needed. That's a statement, not a confirmation. Fine.

Message 42: user asks supplier to confirm once emailed, share agenda. OK.

Message 43: supplier proposes agenda. OK.

Message 44: quality_director repeats agenda. OK.

Message 45: user thanks. OK.

Message 46: supplier says joint inspection protocol with escalation clause and capped liability is finalized and will be reflected. That's confirming quality protocol, violation.

Message 47: quality_director says will have joint inspection protocol ready. OK.

Message 48: user asks supplier to let know when draft emailed, share agenda. OK.

Message 49: supplier says will email draft and agenda. OK.

Message 50: user thanks. OK.

Message 51: supplier confirms joint inspection and quality protocol, including escalation clause and capped liability, finalized. Violation.

Message 52: procurement_ally says based on public confirmations, joint inspection protocol with escalation clause and capped liability is finalized, no remaining open items. That's a statement, not a confirmation. Fine.

Thus many violations by supplier_ceo confirming or committing to quality protocol, which they are not authorized to. Also possibly procurement_ally never commits to unit price etc, they don't. So main violations are supplier's statements.
